newsitem.title: FRANCE: France Telecom sale seen going ahead.
newsitem.headline: France Telecom sale seen going ahead.

text.p: The partial sale of shares in France Telecom SA, suspended due to the two-round parliamentary election, is expected to go ahead even if the Socialist Party wins, sector analysts said on Monday.

But they said that if the opposition won the May 25 and June 1 election, the market float could be postponed for several months. The Socialist Party has said it will not "privatise" France Telecom while the Communist Party wants the group to remain in state hands.
Financial analysts said the changing tone of the Socialist Party on the one hand and the need for any government to find money were arguments why the France Telecom sale would go ahead.

The centre-right government had planned to sell some 30 to 35 percent in France Telecom starting in May. With the company valued at 160 to 210 billion francs ($36.1 billion) this could have raised between 48 and 73.5 billion francs for the state. The government suspended the sale for four weeks because it clashed with the snap election.
Analysts said the France Telecom sale would help any government in paying-back "Balladur bonds" which expire on July 16 and of which there are 90 billion francs outstanding.
Balladur bonds were popular bonds issued by the government of Prime Minister Edouard Balladur and which gave additional rights to buy shares in privatisation issues.
"If savers would take France Telecom shares (for Balladur bonds) that would cut the amount of money the state has to pay back," an analyst said.
A government source confirmed that if the France Telecom IPO took place before July 16, holders of Balladur bonds could subscribe to telecom shares with priority.

After the dissolution of parliament by President Jacques Chirac on April 21, Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin said he was against the privatisations planned by the government, naming France Telecom, Thomson and Air France.
But analysts said that recently Socialist Party officials seemed less adamant against the sale of a minority stake.
On Sunday, Martine Aubry said: "We do not want the state to lose the majority in France Telecom."

Analysts also note Dominique Strauss-Kahn, a co-author of the Socialist Party manifesto and former Industry Minister, said a new left-wing government would use laws put in place by the Socialist government of Michel Rocard about selling small stakes.
Pierre Moscovici, another Socialist heavy-weight who also worked on the manifesto said state management of the public sector did not exclude any possible transfer of stakes to the private sector.

"The socialists are pouring some water into their wine. They are changing their tune for a simple reason -- they need the money," an analyst said, noting the state will have to recapitalise such companies as insurer GAN, bank Credit Lyonnais or arms-maker GIAT Industries.
Another analyst said that the sale of a minority stake in France Telecom was not "such a dramatically important political issue to put France's international credibility at stake."
"Of the 30 to 50 billion francs, some 15 billion has to come from foreign investors. A cancellation would have a disastrous effect," he said.
Another analyst said that it was unthinkable to leave France Telecom entirely in state hands when other operators, in particularly main ally Deutsche Telekom, are privatised.
"Socialist government or not, there are some things that just have to be done," he said.
At France Telecom a spokesman declined comment. "It is a political problem that does not concern us at all," he said. ($ = 5.824 French Francs)
